text: Belgian license plates should have a red tint visible through the blur because they use red text on a white license plate.

clues.title: French Speaking Belgium
text: You can see French in the southern part of Belgium (Wallonia) and both French and Flemish in the the capital of Brussels.

clues.title: Stop sign: Flanders and Brussels bus stop signs
text: Bus stop signs in Flanders (and Brussels) have a white rectangle at the top. In Wallonia they will have a yellow top.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Stop sign: Wallonia bus stop sign
text: Bus stop signs in Flanders (and Brussels) have a white rectangle at the top. In Wallonia they will have a yellow top.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Roadlines
text: Belgium uses all white road lines, these can be continuous or broken.
Roads are often accompanied by bike lanes on both sides.
**NOTE:** Bikes and cycling lanes are most common in the Netherlands, but they can be often seen in Belgium as well.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Ardennes
text: The Ardennes, located in the southeast part of Belgium, have a very distinct landscape. You can see a lot of steep hills, dense forests, and valleys.
NOTE: The Ardennes extend partially into France, Luxembourg, and Germany.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Coastal Plain
text: The coastal plain is extremely flat and consists of so-called polders, which are man-made fields at or below sea level, surrounded by many waterways. This landscape is situated near the North Sea coast, as well as near the western part of the border with the Netherlands, particularly around Antwerp.
NOTE: This part of Belgium is especially often confused with the Netherlands.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Plate: Red License Plates
text: Licence plates in Belgium use red text.
You can recognise this distinct colour even through the blur.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Square Poles
text: Most poles in Belgium are concrete, square shaped, and have tiny holes running up them.
They often have small metal wrappings around them.
The second most common type of pole has oval-shaped holes.
The small metal wrappings can be found in France as well.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Double Gutters
text: Almost all roads (big or small) in Belgium use gutters on both sides.
This is much less common in neighbouring countries.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Bollard: Bollards
text: Belgium uses white bollards with a yellow rectangular reflector on the front and white on the back.
A second type of bollard is dark brown with two red stripes at the top.
Denmark uses similar white bollards, but they have a red stripe at the top and the reflector is not rectangular.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Guardrail: Yellow Reflectors
text: Belgium uses A-type guardrails with yellow reflectors.
In Europe, only Spain, Andorra, and Belgium use these reflectors.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Concrete Roads
text: A lot of rural roads in Belgium are made out of concrete slabs, almost like you would see in the Philippines or Thailand.
The Netherlands almost never uses concrete slabs for roads.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Sign: Additional Blue Signs
text: Road signs often have an additional small blue sign.
In other European countries, these small signs are usually just white.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Dutch (Flemish)
text: Dutch, often referred to as Flemish within Belgium, is a Germanic language. In Belgium, Dutch is spoken in the northern Flanders region, and alongside French in the capital city of Brussels.
Dutch features a lot of double vowels. Typical letter clusters are **ij, ieuw** and **oe**. “**IJ**“ written as one capitalised letter is also unique to the language.
The Dutch name for street is **straat**.
NOTE: Dutch is the main language of the Netherlands.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Street sign: Brussels (bilingual city)
text: Brussels is the capital city of Belgium and officially bilingual in French and Dutch (Flemish). Brussels street signs include both the French **rue** and Dutch **straat**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: French
text: French is a Romance language closely related to languages like Catalan, Spanish and Italian. In Belgium, French is spoken in the southern Wallonia region, and alongside Dutch in the capital city of Brussels.
The French word for street is **rue**.
French uses these diacritics and special letters:
Accent aigu: **é**
Accent grave: **à, è, ù**
Accent circonflexe: **â, ê, î, ô, û**
Trema: **ë, ï, ü, ÿ**
Ligature: **œ**
Cédille: **ç** with a small hook
In addition, the **-ux** suffix is only found in French.
NOTE: French is also widely spoken in France, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Monaco.
